A proposal for describing connections carefully

Open the links between getting ready, choosing, acting and receiving feedback. Each link raises a question about what connects the steps.

A neat diagram can hide a gap in our understanding. The research marks uncertain or missing connections instead of treating every arrow as an established explanation of the brain.

Open each link to see what would be needed to explain it.

Words used here
feedback
Information about what happened returning to a system and potentially changing what happens next.
agency
A person’s ability to make choices and have a meaningful effect on what happens.
Read the fuller explanation

The relationship-first atlas treats connections as conditional objects. A relation names its source, target, needed inputs, evidence and limits. A possible sequence on paper is not proof that every link is present in a particular biological system.

In this small sequence, readiness, selection, action and feedback each have a role. Open a join to see the question it carries. There is no score for how your own life follows the diagram; the display makes no observation of you.

Negative and unknown relations matter as much as proposed positive ones. They prevent a smooth drawing from claiming a completed explanation. Asking where a process stops being understood can be a way of taking agency seriously.

Where this comes from: What an arrow needs to explain

Typed relationship proposal

A proposal for describing connections carefully

Names what a connection needs and what evidence supports it. A drawn arrow is not proof that the connection exists in a brain.

Read the full source note

Brain relationship algebra

Makes conditional, negative and unresolved relationships explicit. A link needs its inputs and evidence; sequential, parallel and alternative compositions have different meanings. The intention scene is conceptual, not a diagnosis or a new neuroscience finding.
